mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Notary public or commissioner of oaths in the country of origin
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Hague Apostille if the issuing state is an Apostille Convention party; otherwise consular legalization at a Canadian embassy or consulate

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Home-country companies registry or licensed corporate registered agent

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Notarized and, where required by Canadian counsel, authenticated with Apostille or consular legalization

ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory screening of all directors, shareholders, officers, authorized signatories, and individuals with significant control against the OFAC SDN List, UN Security Council Consolidated List, Global Affairs Canada Regulated Persons List, and Public Safety Canada Listed Terrorist Entities under the Criminal Code. Domestic and foreign politically exposed persons (PEPs), their family members, and close associates must be identified, escalated to senior management, and subjected to enhanced due diligence under PCMLTFA requirements. OFAC screening is retained as a commercial contract condition because the target payment rails include Wise B2B and US-dollar wire transfers.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: ServiceOntario – Corporate Name Search for Ontario provincial corporations; Corporations Canada – Online Filing Centre and Federal Corporate Name Reservation for federal CBCA corporations
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: The proposed corporate name must be in English, French, or a bilingual form using Roman script. Accented Roman characters are acceptable. If a desired name originates from a non-Roman script, a transliteration or translation must be provided and reflected in the NUANS search. The name must be distinctive, not misdescriptive, and must not comprise only numerals, a generic business descriptor, or a geographical term without a distinctive element.
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: A reserved NUANS name is valid for 90 days; an extension requires a fresh NUANS search report. If the Director or Corporations Canada rejects the name for confusion, prohibited token, or non-distinctiveness, the applicant must obtain the written refusal reasons within 30 days, file a reconsideration request with the relevant registry, and submit a revised name and new NUANS report. Administrative reconsideration must be exhausted before judicial review. For Ontario provincial corporations, an appeal lies to the Ontario Superior Court of Justice under the OBCA; for federal CBCA corporations, judicial review lies to the Federal Court of Canada.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: Permissible for registered-office purposes in Ontario if the corporate services provider maintains a physical street address in Ontario, accepts service of process, and provides document management services. A P.O. box or bare mailing address is not acceptable. For a remote BPO call center, virtual office arrangements do not by themselves create a Canadian permanent establishment or tax residence; however, CRA and FINTRAC will expect that underlying corporate records, UBO/ISC registers, and call-center operational records are accessible at or from the registered office on demand.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: 2–5% annual probability for a standard-risk, non-licensed remote BPO call center; the likelihood rises to approximately 15–20% if a UBO, PEP, OFAC, or adverse-media flag is triggered, or if there is a mismatch between declared registered office and actual business substance.

incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Ontario Business Corporations Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. B.16, ss. 4-15 (incorporation), s. 17 (registered office), s. 19 (articles), s. 23 (share consideration), s. 121 (directors); Ontario Corporations Information Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.39, s. 2 (notice filing)
incorporation_legal_framework.competent_registry_authority: Ontario Ministry of Public and Business Service Delivery, Companies and Personal Property Security Branch (CPPSB); online portal: Ontario Business Registry
incorporation_legal_framework.statutory_filing_instrument: Articles of Incorporation (Form 1) under the OBCA, filed electronically via the Ontario Business Registry
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: No statutory minimum paid-up capital; the Articles may authorize shares with no par value. No escrow account is required. Consideration for issued shares may consist of money, property, promissory note, or past service performed, per OBCA s. 23(2).
incorporation_legal_framework.pro_forma_first_board_resolution_en: RESOLVED THAT the first directors accept the subscriptions for one common share per initial subscriber at a price of $1.00 CDN per share, and issue such shares fully paid and non-assessable upon receipt of consideration; RESOLVED THAT the registered office of the Corporation is hereby fixed and adopted as the address stated in the Articles of Incorporation, and the directors are authorized to file the Initial Notice and any prescribed forms with the Ontario Business Registry; RESOLVED THAT the following officers are appointed: Chief Executive Officer, Chief Financial Officer, and Corporate Secretary, each to serve at the pleasure of the Board; RESOLVED THAT management is directed to open a corporate bank account, maintain corporate records, and complete all post-incorporation registrations with the Canada Revenue Agency and the Ontario Ministry of Finance.

step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Ontario Business Registry / Authorized NUANS search provider
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Submit a proposed corporate name through a NUANS pre-screening. Verify distinctiveness and that the name complies with OBCA regulations. If the name is clear, obtain a NUANS report and reserve the name for 90 days, or elect to proceed as a numbered company to avoid delay.
required_dossiers: NUANS preliminary search report if corporate name is used
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the name is refused or confusingly similar, file a new name request with additional search evidence or incorporate using a numbered name and adopt a trade name later.

step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Ontario Business Registry, Ministry of Public and Business Service Delivery
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Complete Form 1 Articles of Incorporation online, including full legal name, registered office address, share structure, first directors, and any restrictions on business activities. Pay the statutory filing fee and submit the Notice of Directors and Notice of Registered Office simultaneously.
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Ministry queries the filing, the incorporator must file amended Articles and re-submit within the statutory correction period; any defective director consent must be re-executed and attached.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Registered Office and First Directors Designation Confirmation
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Confirm the adopted registered office address in Ontario exactly as stated in the Articles. Ensure the office is open during ordinary business hours and accessible for service of process. Confirm the first directors are at least 18 years old, not bankrupt, and individually consent to act.
required_dossiers: Consent to Act as First Director forms
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the registered office is rejected, file a Change of Registered Office notice immediately and re-submit the required municipal address proof.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: First Organizational Meeting and Board Resolution
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Board of Directors of the Corporation
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Convene the first meeting of incorporators and directors. Adopt the pro forma First Board Resolution: confirm share subscriptions and issuance, adopt a general by-law, appoint officers, authorize banking resolutions, approve corporate seal if any, and order the preparation of minute books and share certificates.
required_dossiers: Waiver of notice or unanimous consent
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If a director is unavailable, secure a signed unanimous shareholder consent or reconvene the meeting with proper notice; any irregular issuance of shares must be ratified by a subsequent board resolution.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Tax Registration and Business Number Activation
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) and Ontario Ministry of Finance
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Register the corporation with the CRA to obtain a nine-digit Business Number (BN). Select the relevant CRA accounts: GST/HST, corporate income tax, payroll source deductions if employees are hired. Register for the Ontario Corporations Tax account through the Ontario Business Registry, and obtain any municipal business licence if the local by-law so requires.
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If CRA rejects the business number application due to director identity mismatch, correct the personal information and re-file through the CRA Business Registration Online portal within 30 days.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Corporate Records, Minute Book, and Annual Return Compliance
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Corporation's Registered Office / Ontario Business Registry
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Establish and maintain the statutory minute book at the registered office containing: Articles of Incorporation, by-laws, board and shareholder minutes, share ledger, and transfers register. File the Initial Return with CPPSB within 5 business days after incorporation and file the annual return with the Ontario Business Registry on each anniversary date.
required_dossiers: Minute book binding and divider set
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Initial Return is late or rejected, file a late amended return immediately and pay the prescribed late-filing fee; missing share certificates must be cancelled and re-issued by board resolution.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.competent_industrial_authority: No dedicated industrial licensing board applies to BPO call centres; workplace safety oversight is provided by the Ontario Ministry of Labour, Immigration, Training and Skills Development (MLITSD).
industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.operating_license_title: No statutory operating or manufacturing permit is required for a remote multilingual BPO and call-centre service under Ontario law; a local municipal business licence may be required depending on the municipality where the physical office is located.

environmental_impact_assessment_eia.agency_name: Ontario Ministry of the Environment, Conservation and Parks (MECP)
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.classification_tier: Exempt - the activity is an unoccupied remote call-centre / BPO operation that does not trigger a full Environmental Impact Assessment; general compliance obligations under the Ontario Environmental Protection Act and municipal sewer by-laws apply.
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.discharge_and_emissions_standards: No industrial wastewater, VOC, or point-source air emissions are generated. If an emergency diesel generator is installed or office HVAC equipment creates local discharges, comply with O. Reg. 419/05 (Local Air Quality) and O. Reg. 347/90 (waste management). Office sanitary wastewater must connect to municipal sewer under the applicable municipal sewer use by-law with normal domestic-strength discharge.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.civil_defense_and_occupational_clearance: Fire safety certification under the Ontario Fire Code (O. Reg. 213/07), including fire evacuation plans, fire extinguishers and alarm inspection. Structural load inspection under the Ontario Building Code for safe office occupancy. Occupational health clearance under the Occupational Health and Safety Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. O.1, including workplace hazard assessment, ergonomic workstation assessment, electrical safety and emergency preparedness for a call-centre workplace.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (Agence du revenu du Canada) — Business Registration Online (BRO) portal and My Business Account (MBA) digital services portal; Ontario Ministry of Finance for provincial corporate tax, which is administered and collected by the CRA under the Canada-Ontario Tax Collection Agreement
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: Non-resident corporations carrying on business in Canada must obtain a 9-digit Business Number (BN) from the CRA by filing Form RC1 (Request for a Business Number) or Form RC1A (Request for a Business Number – Non-Resident), or online via the BRO portal. The application requires: (i) certificate of incorporation or equivalent foreign registration document; (ii) full legal name, registered office address, and directors' names/addresses; (iii) a Canadian contact address or authorized representative (Form RC391); (iv) description of planned activities (NAICS 561422 / ISIC 7820). Program accounts established simultaneously or subsequently include: corporate income tax (RC), GST/HST (RT), payroll (RP), and import/export (RM) accounts. A BN and RT program account must be activated before the first taxable supply is made; the CRA normally issues the BN within 5-10 business days for paper filings and immediately for online BRO filings.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.default_entity_tax_classification: Entity_Level_Taxation; territorial scope: a resident corporation (incorporated federally or in Ontario) is taxable on worldwide income under ITA s. 2(1); a non-resident corporation is taxable only on Canadian-source business and capital gains under ITA s. 2(3) and Part XIV branch tax; no tax-exempt zones exist in Ontario; the Canadian corporation is not eligible for pass-through treatment.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: Voluntary GST/HST registration election for small suppliers (ETA s. 240); section 211 election for closely related corporations to treat otherwise taxable supplies as non-taxable; section 150 election to treat a supply as taxable even if exempt; Quick Method of Accounting election (ETA s. 227); streamlined accounting for non-residents; for income tax: ITA s. 216 election (non-resident net basis on Canadian rental/timber income), ITA s. 219 election (branch tax with additional property allowance, Form T2046), ITA s. 219.1 branch tax exemption election; hybrid mismatch rules under ITA ss. 18.2, 18.3 and 20.2 (as amended, effective for 2023+ transactions) apply to deny deductions on certain hybrid arrangements — Canada has no US-style 'check-the-box' regime.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: GST/HST (Goods and Services Tax / Harmonized Sales Tax) — administered federally by the CRA; Ontario participates in the HST under the Comprehensive Integrated Tax Coordination Agreement
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: CAD 30,000 in annual worldwide taxable supplies (small supplier threshold, ETA s. 148(1)); a non-resident carrying on business in Canada (including a permanent establishment in Ontario) must register for GST/HST once worldwide taxable revenues exceed CAD 30,000 per calendar quarter or trailing four-quarter period; registration is mandatory within 29 days of breach; voluntary registration is available for exporters and others; a call center whose only supplies are zero-rated exports may still be required to register if it carries on business in Canada and crosses the threshold.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: No mandatory government real-time fiscal clearance, API clearance, or digital stamping exists in Canada. The CRA permits electronic invoicing in standard formats (PDF, XML, EDI) and is a participant in the voluntary Pan-Canadian e-invoicing framework (Peppol-based PINT), but adoption is non-mandatory. Invoices must meet statutory content requirements (ETA s. 169(1) and Sched. VI, Part II): vendor legal name, BN, date, invoice number, description of supply, and HST paid/payable. Records and invoices must be retained for six years in either English or French.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Section 25 of Part V, Schedule VI to the ETA zero-rates a supply of a service made to a non-resident recipient where the non-resident is not registered for GST/HST and the service is not: (a) supplied to a person who is in Canada at the time the service is rendered; (b) in connection with real property situated in Canada; (c) in connection with tangible personal property situated in Canada at the time the service is rendered; (d) a service of acting as an agent, a service in respect of insolvency, or advisory/consulting services (subject to exceptions); or (e) a supply of a service rendered to a non-resident who is registered under the ETA. For a remote BPO call center (ISIC 7820), zero-rating is achievable when: (i) the contractual recipient is a foreign principal/client not registered for GST/HST; (ii) the call center services are not rendered to Canadian end-customers (i.e., call traffic exclusively serves foreign consumers or business clients outside Canada); (iii) no Canadian real property or goods located in Canada are the subject of the service. If the BPO answers calls from Canadian customers of the foreign principal, the service is generally considered supplied to a person in Canada and is taxable at 13% HST; in such cases, the BPO must charge HST unless another exemption or the 'prescribed services' rules apply. The BPO may claim input tax credits (ITCs) for GST/HST paid on business inputs only if it is registered and the supplies are commercial; zero-rated exporters are entitled to full ITC recovery through routine GST/HST returns (no separate export refund application).
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Canadian Export Declaration (Form B13A via the CBSA Canadian Export Reporting System / G7 EDI) — applicable only to tangible goods; for pure BPO services no B13A is filed, but a service description and geographic scope statement is required

Commercial Invoice and Bill of Lading / Air Waybill (for goods) or BPO Master Service Agreement with the non-resident client stipulating place of performance, recipient status, and absence of Canadian end-user service

Inward Remittance Certificate (bank/FX proof of payment in CAD equivalent) plus the non-resident client's written certification of non-registration for GST/HST and foreign tax status, together with invoices, payment trail, call records, and contracts demonstrating zero-rated export treatment
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: CRA audit scrutiny is detailed for service exports: the CRA may reassess GST/HST within four years of the filing date (ETA s. 296(1)), with no limitation period for misrepresentation, neglect, or fraud (ETA s. 298(4)). If zero-rating is denied, the taxpayer is liable for the full 13% HST on all disputed invoices plus compounded daily interest under ETA s. 280. A gross negligence penalty of up to 25% of the tax amount applies under ETA s. 285.1, and for egregious conduct by corporations a stricter penalty of up to 50% of the net tax amount may be imposed for transactions occurring after 2022 (ETA s. 285.1(2.1)). Knowingly making false statements for zero-rating can constitute tax evasion, leading to prosecution under ETA s. 327, fines of up to CAD 200,000 and/or imprisonment for up to two years. CRA may also claw back ITCs previously allowed and reassess corporate income tax where the export structure lacks commercial substance.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada (Banque du Canada), established under the Bank of Canada Act (1934). Foreign-exchange intervention and official international reserves management sit with the Bank of Canada in coordination with the Department of Finance Canada. Anti-money-laundering and cross-border electronic-funds-transfer supervision are administered by FINTRAC (Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada) under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act (PCMLTFA), while the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) administers tax-related non-resident remittance reporting and corporate account registrations.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: Canada maintains a free-floating exchange-rate regime with full de jure and de facto convertibility between the Canadian dollar (CAD) and all major currencies. There are no exchange controls, no central-bank approval requirement for capital movements, and no restrictions on current-account payments under the Currency Act, the Bank of Canada Act, or the former Foreign Exchange Control Regulations (repealed 1951). Share capital injections, shareholder loans, loan repayments, dividends, interest, royalties, management fees, and BPO service revenues may all be transferred freely into and out of Ontario-based corporate accounts. The only practical hurdles are fiscal and documentary: non-resident shareholders are subject to Canadian Part XIII withholding tax (statutory 25%, typically treaty-reduced to 5% on dividends for a US parent under the Canada-US Tax Convention), and all cross-border wire transfers of CAD 10,000 or more trigger FINTRAC and Bank of Canada reporting. For a remote BPO call center earning service income from non-resident clients, there is no surviving capital-account restriction on profit remittance; the operative obstacles are source-of-funds evidence, beneficial-ownership disclosure, and the bank's Enhanced Due Diligence (EDD) framework.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: Canada imposes no export-proceeds surrender requirement, no mandatory conversion ratio, and no statutory repatriation timeline. Exporters and cross-border service suppliers (including BPO operators) may retain foreign currency indefinitely in Canadian or offshore deposit accounts and may disburse those balances without Bank of Canada approval. The only binding obligations are reporting-regime duties: (i) under the Bank of Canada's Wire Transfer Reporting Regulations, Canadian financial institutions must report SWIFT wire transfers of CAD 10,000 or more sent or received; (ii) under the PCMLTFA, FINTRAC electronic-funds-transfer reports (EFTR) are required for transactions of CAD 10,000 or more within a 24-hour window; and (iii) the Bank of Canada / Statistics Canada International Transactions Reporting System (ITRS) captures balance-of-payments data on service exports. None of these rules require conversion of USD (or other foreign-currency) receivables into CAD, and no export proceeds need be 'surrendered' to the Bank of Canada.

tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.account_class: Operational Account (CAD and USD clear account); Capital Escrow Account available under a separate custody services agreement
Operational Account (CAD); USD sub-account via TD's US clearing network
Operational Account (CAD and USD); Capital Escrow Account available for subscription proceeds
Operational Account (CAD); international wire-clearing via Scotiabank's global network

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Feasibility: MEDIUM-HIGH as a complementary payment rail; LOW as a primary treasury account. Legal constraints: an offshore digital EMI (e-money institution) must be registered with FINTRAC as a Money Service Business (MSB) under the PCMLTFA in order to provide payment or deposit-like services to Canadian residents; operating without registration is a criminal offense. Wise (Wise Payments Limited / Wise Payments Canada Ltd.) and Payoneer are FINTRAC-registered MSBs and are viable for vendor disbursements, small-value client refunds, and cross-border payroll supplements. The target payment rail 'Wise_B2B' is therefore permissible provided the entity maintains a full-service Schedule I corporate account as the primary sink. The legal constraint is that the corporate operating account must remain at a Schedule I bank because Canadian payroll source deductions (CRA), GST/HST registration, Part XIII withholding on non-resident payments, and T2 corporate filing require a complete Canadian banking relationship. Funds routed through a fintech EMI must be traceable to the corporate bank account; commingling client funds through an unregistered offshore EMI would constitute a FINTRAC red flag and a PCMLTFA violation.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: There is no statutory mandate requiring directors to appear physically at a Canadian bank branch; FINTRAC permits remote identity verification using the 'two-step process' (verification by two distinct KYC methods, e.g., government-issued photo ID plus a utility/account verification) or third-party attestation by a qualified professional (lawyer or accountant). In practice, the Big-5 Schedule I banks will permit fully remote corporate onboarding for a low-risk, Ontario-registered BPO provided that: (i) at least one director or authorized officer holds a Canadian nexus (valid Canadian passport, driver's licence, or permanent-resident card); (ii) the company is CRA-registered with a 9-digit Business Number (BN) and the 'RP' (GST/HST) and 'RC' (payroll) accounts; and (iii) a certified corporate records package is delivered electronically (Certificate of Incorporation, Articles of Incorporation, Ontario Business Information Report, register of directors, beneficial-ownership declaration, and shareholder resolution on account opening). Where no director holds a Canadian nexus, the banks require a physical in-branch interview of the proposed signatory during a verification visit to Ontario, or a notarized/commissioned attestation executed at a Canadian consulate abroad. A hybrid model—remote upload of the KYC bundle followed by a 30-minute video interview with the bank's onboarding officer—is the current standard for Schedule I banks when onboarding a single-purpose, client-funded BPO entity. The account opening forms must designate at least one Canadian-resident agent for service (registered office address in Ontario).

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Underwriting red flag: High-risk jurisdiction counterparty or irregular source-of-funds for the initial share-capital injection (e.g., remitter is a third-party financing entity rather than the registered shareholder, or funds originate from a jurisdiction with weak AML standards).
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: The defense bundle must contain: (1) a certified copy of the board resolution authorizing the capital contribution; (2) a share subscription agreement identifying the subscriber and the exact CAD amount; (3) the remitting shareholder's bank statements covering at least 12 months to evidence accumulation of legitimate funds; (4) audited financial statements of the parent/shareholder (or a CPA-reviewed statement of affairs); (5) a source-of-funds declaration on the bank's FINTRAC-compliant questionnaire; (6) the Ontario Business Information Report and corporate registry extraction confirming the depositor's status as shareholder; and (7) a notarized affidavit attesting to the legitimacy of the funds.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Underwriting red flag: Discrepancy between the registered business purpose and the transactional pattern—e.g., rapid pass-through of third-party payments, frequent round-dollar transfers, or an unusually high volume of incoming wires relative to the invoiced BPO client base.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: The defense bundle must contain: (1) a complete funds-flow diagram showing the contractual chain; (2) executed Master Service Agreements (MSA) with named end-clients for the inbound helpdesk and outbound tele-sales activities (ISIC 7820 / NAICS 561422); (3) a sample of monthly service invoices with matching payment confirmations; (4) the payroll register and outsourced-agent rosters to substantiate operating scale; (5) a written explanation from the entity's Canadian CPA firm describing the operating cycle (billings, receipts, subcontractor disbursements); and (6) screenshots from the bank's monthly surveillance questionnaire showing no unexplained cash accumulation.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Underwriting red flag: Beneficial-ownership opacity or a multi-tiered foreign parent structure with jurisdictions that delay registry disclosure (e.g., LLC chains in certain US states or intermediate holding companies in non-cooperative jurisdictions).
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: The defense bundle must contain: (1) an organizational chart identifying all direct and indirect shareholders up to the ultimate individual beneficial owner; (2) certified foreign registry extracts for each intermediate entity; (3) the entity's Articles of Incorporation and Register of Directors; (4) a beneficial-ownership (BO) declaration form completed per FINTRAC's reporting guidance; (5) the CRA Business Number confirmation; and (6) a directors' resolution ratifying the BO disclosure and committing to ongoing notification of any 25-percent-or-greater ownership change.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Underwriting red flag: Large-volume outbound disbursements to high-risk jurisdictions (e.g., payments to offshore BPO subcontractors in jurisdictions with limited AML enforcement) while the entity's stated business is 'low-risk inbound helpdesk'.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: The defense bundle must contain: (1) executed subcontracting agreements with each foreign payee; (2) the payee's own KYC/incorporation documents; (3) evidence of services actually rendered (time logs, QA call recordings, ticketing-system extracts, performance dashboards); (4) a list of beneficiary names and bank identifiers to support the bank's payee screening; (5) the entity's written AML/ATF policy and its third-party due-diligence procedure; and (6) annual CPA-reviewed financial statements reconciling outbound disbursements to invoiced client revenue.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Compliant protocol: The non-resident parent or shareholder initiates an outbound SWIFT wire (MT103) from its home-country bank to the entity's Schedule I operational account in Ontario. Canada does not apply China-style fixed purpose-code matrices; the remitter includes a narrative description that the bank maps to IMF BPM6 classifications. An equity injection must be described as 'Share capital contribution — [Corporate Name], Ontario, Canada' and mapped to BPM6 'Direct Investment — Equity Capital' (line DI2); a shareholder loan must be described as 'Shareholder loan — [Corporate Name]' and mapped to 'Direct Investment — Other Capital'. Supporting verification that must accompany the credit: (i) a certified copy of the board/shareholder resolution authorizing the contribution; (ii) the share subscription record or share-certificate ledger entry; (iii) the parent's audited financial statements or 12-month bank statements evidencing the legitimate source of funds; (iv) a FINTRAC-compliant source-of-funds questionnaire if the amount exceeds CAD 10,000; and (v) an Ontario corporate registry search confirming the remitter's status as shareholder. The receiving bank reports the wire under the Bank of Canada's Wire Transfer Reporting Regulations (CAD 10,000 or more) and files a FINTRAC EFTR. The funds must be booked to share capital and reflected in the first T2 corporate return and the audited financial statements. Any mismatch between the remitter name and the registered shareholder triggers an automatic EDD review and a potential 5-business-day hold. To avoid 'structuring' allegations, the full intended contribution must be remitted as a single, openly-described wire and never split into tranches below CAD 10,000.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Primary clearing rail: SWIFT MT103 for cross-border supplier payments (telecom platforms, telephony-infrastructure licences, software-as-a-service subscriptions, subcontracted offshore BPO capacity, and vendor invoices). For a service-based BPO, Commercial Letters of Credit (UCP 600) are rarely applicable and are reserved for physical-goods procurement (servers, headsets, telephony hardware); a revocable or irrevocable LC can be opened through the Toronto-based Schedule I bank with a confirming bank in the supplier's jurisdiction. Domestic CAD clearing options: the Large Value Transfer System (LVTS) for same-day high-value payments and the Real-Time Rail (RTR) for retail-speed credits. For USD-denominated vendor contracts, the entity should maintain a USD clear account with the same Schedule I bank to avoid spot-conversion leakage; USD wires clear over CHIPS or Fedwire for same-day settlement. Payroll disbursements are executed through the bank's payroll module with CRA source deductions (income tax, CPP, EI) remitted via the predefined 'RC' account and reconciled on the T4/NR4 filings. Outbound dividends to a non-resident shareholder are remitted via MT103 after the bank withholds Part XIII tax at the applicable treaty rate (e.g., 5% on dividends to a qualifying US parent under the Canada-US Treaty); the bank files the NR4 information return with the CRA and remits the withheld tax. Management fees and subcontractor payments to non-residents are similarly paid via MT103 with description codes aligned to the underlying service contract, and the entity must file the appropriate T-slips and Part XIII returns where required.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Deliverable FX Forwards (outright USD/CAD forwards): physically settled via CLS or bilateral same-day netting; the standard hedge for USD-indexed BPO client receipts over 1- to 12-month tenors.

Cross-Currency Swaps (FX swaps and rollover swaps): permissible for aligning a long-term CAD shareholder loan injected from a US parent with USD-denominated operating expenses over multi-year horizons.

Non-Deliverable Forwards (NDF): permissible for hedging exposures to restricted or non-convertible currencies (e.g., INR, PHP, MXN) when disbursing to offshore subcontractors; CAD/USD NDFs are unnecessary because CAD is fully deliverable.

Plain-vanilla FX options (call/put spreads): permissible, though conservatively optional, for a low-risk BPO treasury with predictable USD revenue; no regulatory pre-clearance is required because OTC FX derivatives are outside securities registration in Canada.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Federal Annual Return under the Canada Business Corporations Act (CBCA), filed online or Form 4027 by a director/officer
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Corporations Canada, Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 60 days of the annual anniversary of incorporation; e.g., incorporation on 15 March requires filing no later than 14 May of each year
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Two consecutive years of non-filing triggers administrative dissolution (CBCA s. 212); offenders are liable on summary conviction to a fine of up to CAD 5,000 (approx USD 3,650) (CBCA s. 261); filing is also a prerequisite for a Certificate of Compliance for foreign operations

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Ontario Annual Report for Extra-Provincial Corporation under the Corporations Information Act (Form 2 / online)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Ontario Companies and Personal Property Security Branch (CPSB), Ministry of Public and Business Service Delivery
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 60 days of the anniversary of the extra-provincial registration in Ontario; registration anniversary e.g. 1 April requires filing by 31 May
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Revocation of Ontario registration after administrative notice; unregistered corporations lose the right to enforce contracts or sue in Ontario courts and may incur fines up to CAD 5,000 (Corporations Information Act s. 15)

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: T2 Corporation Income Tax Return; the federal return incorporates Ontario Corporations Tax liability under the federal-provincial tax collection agreement (ITA s. 150; Ontario Corporations Tax Act)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Not later than 6 months after fiscal year-end; a 31 December year-end is due by 30 June
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late-filing penalty: 5% of unpaid federal/Ontario tax plus 1% per full month up to 12 months, with a CAD 100 (approx USD 73) minimum penalty on nil-return filers (ITA s. 162); 3 consecutive years of non-filing may trigger CRA administrative dissolution; directors liable for unremitted corporate tax under ITA s. 227.1

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual GST/HST Return (if the corporation qualifies for annual filing under the Excise Tax Act elections for small suppliers with qualifying revenue under CAD 1,500,000)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 3 months after the fiscal year-end; a 31 December year-end is due by 31 March of the following year
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: ETA s. 280 penalty: 6% of net tax owing plus 1% per full month late; late-filed nil returns attract CAD 250 (approx USD 183) minimum penalty; repeated defaults may be prosecuted as a due-diligence offence

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: CBCA s. 161 mandates an auditor for all corporations unless the corporation is a non-distributing (private) corporation and all shareholders consent in writing to dispense with the audit (CBCA s. 163). No monetary or revenue threshold applies to private CBCA corporations; any single shareholder refusal to waive requires a mandatory independent audit. Ontario extra-provincial registration does not impose an additional audit condition.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: IFRS (Part I CPA Canada Handbook) for publicly accountable enterprises; ASPE (Part II) for private enterprises; financial statements in either framework are accepted for CBCA shareholder approval and CRA corporate tax filing purposes, with the T2 return computed on the Income Tax Act basis.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: CBCA s. 21.1 et seq. requires a register of individuals with significant control (ISC), defined as owning/controlling 25% or more of the voting shares or fair market value, or de facto control. The ISC register must be updated within 15 days of any change and kept for 6 years after an individual ceases to have significant control. Effective 22 January 2024, Corporations Canada requires ISC information to be submitted with the annual return and confirmed accurate as of the filing date; transfers >25% or share dispositions must be simultaneously recorded in the Register of Transfers and the ISC register before the annual confirmation is rendered.
mandatory_on_site_statutory_registers: Register of Officers (if officers are appointed)
Register of Individuals with Significant Control (ISC) / UBO Register

corporate_income_tax_regime.statutory_headline_rate: 26.5% combined general corporate rate (Federal 15% + Ontario 11.5%); 12.2% combined rate for a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) claiming the Small Business Deduction (SBD) on the first CAD 500,000 of active business income (Federal 9% + Ontario 3.2%)
corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: No material BPO-specific tax holiday exists in Ontario. A non-resident-controlled corporation is not a CCPC and therefore cannot claim the SBD, leaving a flat 26.5% effective combined rate on Ontario-source active income. Standard commercial deductions (staff wages, telecommunications, software, rent, subcontracted offshore BPO costs) reduce the tax base. Ontario Manufacturing and Processing Profits Tax Credit (10% M&P rate) does not apply to call center services; SR&ED benefits generally unavailable for routine BPO operations.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: T2 Corporation Income Tax Return; transmitted to the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) via CRA-approved EFILE software, or paper filing for nil returns; Ontario corporate income tax is administered and collected by the CRA under the Corporate Tax Administration Ontario model and reported on the same T2 return
tax_return_filing_anatomy.reporting_frequency: Annual; tax instalments are required monthly or quarterly throughout the fiscal year (monthly for large corporations and most non-CCPCs)
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: T2 return due within 6 months after the fiscal year-end. Final tax balance due within 2 months after fiscal year-end (3 months for a CCPC that claimed the SBD in the preceding year); the foreign-owned BPO corporation therefore generally meets a 2-month payment deadline and a 6-month filing deadline.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Legal corporate name, CRA business number (BN), registered office jurisdiction (Ontario), fiscal year-end, industry code (NAICS 561422 / ISIC 7820), and directors' names and addresses.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Enter the Canadian BN; non-resident directors provide their home jurisdiction address and, if applicable, an ITN (Individual Tax Number); the entity must identify its non-resident parent as the controlling shareholder.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Taxable income after application of Part I adjustments, loss carryovers, and the deductibility of business expenses (wages, occupancy, telecom, purchased BPO services).
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Claim only arm's-length or properly documented intercompany expenses; deductibility of management fees paid to a non-resident is limited to the extent the services were actually rendered and a reasonable mark-up was charged; respect Canada's earnings-stripping and thin-capitalization limits.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Federal corporate income tax computed at 15% (general) on Line 340 taxable income.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident-controlled corporations cannot claim the federal SBD rate of 9%; apply 15%, then compute the provincial tax below.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Ontario corporate income tax computed at 11.5% (general rate) on Ontario-allocated taxable income using the Ontario allocation formula (average of Ontario gross revenue, Ontario wages/salaries, and Ontario taxable paid capital ratios).
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: For a BPO fully staffed and managed in Ontario, allocate 100% to Ontario; do not under-allocate revenue to offshore affiliates without factual substance and contemporaneous transfer pricing documentation.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Claims non-capital losses carried back 3 years or forward 20 years; balance-due reductions and refundable/refund claims are tracked by the CRA.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident-owned corporations may carry forward losses for the full 20-year period; maintain continuity of ownership and business to preserve loss availability on a future ownership change.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Discloses transactions with non-residents at non-arm's length, including BPO service fees paid to or received from offshore affiliates; T106 information return must be filed with the same transaction details.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Mandatory where the aggregate value of connected transactions with non-residents exceeds CAD 1,000,000 per taxation year; continue reporting even if no transfer pricing adjustment is claimed; state the transfer pricing method used.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late T2 filing: 5% of unpaid tax plus 1% per complete month (maximum 12 months); repeat offender: 10% plus 2% per month (maximum 20 months) under ITA s.162; arrears interest compounded daily at CRA's prescribed rate plus 4% per annum (2024 arrears rate approximately 9%); unpaid instalments attract additional penalties under ITA s.163.1; failure to file T106: CAD 25 per day (minimum CAD 100, maximum CAD 2,500) under s.162(10.1), rising to CAD 100 per day (maximum CAD 12,500) for gross negligence.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: T106 Information Return for Non-Arm's-Length Transactions with Non-Residents; filed with the CRA in parallel with the T2 (mandatory electronic filing for large corporations)
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: Due within 6 months after the Canadian corporation's fiscal year-end (same due date as the T2 return)

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Part I - Identification of Non-Arm's-Length Persons
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Names, addresses, country of residence, and relationship of each non-resident affiliate (offshore BPO parent or sister company) engaged in cross-border transactions.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Include the non-resident parent and any offshore call-center subcontractor; provide their foreign tax identification numbers and complete ownership structures.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Part V - Transactions and Transfer Pricing Method
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Quantifies each category of transaction (purchase of services, management fees, royalties, interest, dividends paid) and records the transfer pricing method applied.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: For inbound helpdesk BPO services, apply CUP or TNMM with a documented profit level indicator; for outbound tele-sales, a comparable cost-plus or TNMM analysis is typical; describe the specific method and comparables relied upon.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late/non-filing of T106: CAD 25 per day, maximum CAD 2,500 (basic); CAD 100 per day, maximum CAD 12,500 (gross negligence); habitual failure adds CAD 100 per month per form up to CAD 500 per month; separate transfer pricing penalty under ITA s.247(3) of 10% of the net upward adjustment applies when the adjustment exceeds the lesser of CAD 5,000,000 or 10% of gross revenue and no contemporaneous documentation exists.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: 25% under ITA s.212(2), levied on all dividends paid by the Canadian corporation to non-resident shareholders
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: To apply a reduced DTA rate, the beneficial owner must (i) certify beneficial ownership and residency using CRA Form NR301 (if invoking the Canada-US treaty, also provide Form W-8BEN-E), (ii) obtain and deliver upon request a Certificate of Residency (TRC) issued by the home tax authority (e.g., IRS Form 6166 for US residents), and (iii) hold the shares beneficially without back-to-back conduit arrangements. The Canadian payor then reduces withholding at source under the applicable treaty (typical corporate shareholder rate: 5% for 10%+ voting interest; 15% portfolio). If the full 25% statutory rate was withheld because certification was late, the non-resident must file CRA Form NR7 within 2 years after the end of the calendar year in which the dividend was paid to claim a refund; the CRA may request audited financial statements and a share register to verify beneficial ownership.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Royalties: statutory 25% WHT under ITA s.212(1)(d); typical DTA rate 10% (Canada-US treaty: 0% for most copyright royalties, 10% for other royalties; Canada-Ontario does not grant separate relief). Interest: statutory 25% WHT under ITA s.212(1)(b); typical DTA rate 10% for non-arm's-length/related-party interest (Canada-US treaty exempts most arm's-length interest, including interest paid to a related US lender, provided the recipient is the beneficial owner); back-to-back loan arrangements are re-characterized under ITA s.212(3.1).

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: Canada does not impose a strict OECD three-tier (master/file/local) threshold; however, contemporaneous transfer pricing documentation aligned with CRA Information Circular IC 87-2R and the OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines is required whenever the aggregate value of cross-border connected transactions with non-residents exceeds CAD 1,000,000 in a taxation year. For the remote BPO call center, the documentation must include a functional analysis, risk profile, and benchmarked arm's-length margin; typical full-cost-plus margins for comparable BPO/call-center services range from 5% to 15% depending on the functional profile and comparables selected.
approved_arm_length_methodologies: CUP - Comparable Uncontrolled Price (used for defined per-seat or per-minute BPO fees)
Resale Price Method (rare for BPO services)
Cost Plus Method (primary for outbound tele-sales with low asset intensity)
TNMM - Transactional Net Margin Method (primary for inbound helpdesk and call-center services)
Profit Split Method (only for highly integrated operations involving valuable intangibles)
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: Canada has no UAE-style Economic Substance Regulations; substance and profit attribution are instead policed through ITA s.247 (arm's length rule), ITA s.245 (GAAR), the PE article of each applicable treaty (OECD Article 5/7 attribution), the treaties' principal purpose test (PPT) under the MLI, and the Canada-US treaty's Limitation on Benefits clause. The Ontario BPO entity must demonstrate real decision-making, staffing, risk absorption, and premises in Ontario; a bare invoicing conduit that lacks substance will be denied treaty benefits and re-attributed profit at the CRA's discretion. Additional anti-erosion rules apply: thin capitalization (debt-to-equity of 1.5:1 for specified non-resident debt), the excessive interest and financing expenses limitation (EIFEL) capturing 30% EBITDA-based interest disallowance for large groups, and Ontario Employer Health Tax (1.95% on payroll above CAD 1,000,000).

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Invoicing the Canadian BPO entity for fictitious offshore 'management services' or call-center subcontracted work that was never performed; deliberately understating Ontario taxable income or overstating intercompany deductions.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Gross negligence penalty of 50% of the understated tax under ITA s.163(2); criminal prosecution under ITA s.239 with fines of 50% to 200% of the evaded tax and imprisonment up to 2 years; unlimited re-assessment period for fraud; Ontario parallel penalties and interest.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors and officers are personally prosecutable as authors of the evasion; courts may impose civil restitution orders equal to the evaded tax, bail conditions and court-ordered travel bans with passport surrender, and custodial sentences. The CRA may also pierce the veil under ITA s.160 for transfers of assets to shareholders or related parties.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Non-Filing of T2, T106, and Ontario Allocation
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Failure to file the T2 return or T106 information return within 6 months of the fiscal year-end, or deliberately misstating the Ontario allocation factor to shift profit to an offshore affiliate.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Late filing penalties (5%/1% per month), arrears interest, T106 penalties (CAD 25 to 12,500), and allocation-revision assessments; the CRA can nullify the offshore allocation and assess 100% of the profit in Ontario.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors remain jointly and severally liable for unremitted employee source deductions and GST/HST held in trust under ITA s.227.1; willful non-filing is prosecuted as evasion, engaging civil restitution, travel bans, and imprisonment for directing officers.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Transfer Pricing Mispricing of BPO Services
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Charging the Canadian entity an inflated offshore call-center fee without a benchmarked arm's-length margin, or using a consistent loss-making or zero-margin arrangement that fails the TNMM/Cost Plus standard.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: CRA transfer pricing adjustment to arm's-length results; ITA s.247(3) penalty of 10% of the net adjustment; interest accrues from the original due date; double taxation unless a competent-authority MAP is pursued.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who approved the les-than-arm's-length pricing may be assessed personally if they signed the false T106/T2 return with gross negligence; exposure includes restitution, fines, and travel restrictions pending criminal proceedings.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Using the Ontario corporation as a conduit entity that lacks economic substance, employees, or premises, with the main purpose of obtaining Canada-U.S. or other DTA benefits and reducing the 25% Part XIII WHT.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Denial of treaty benefits under the MLI PPT or the Canada-U.S. LOB article; full 25% withholding re-applied; GAAR re-characterization, and the CRA may deem the offshore parent to have a Canadian permanent establishment, exposing it to Canadian tax and branch penalties.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors of both the Canadian and foreign entities face joint assessments under ITA s.160, civil restitution of the unpaid WHT, and, where documents are fabricated, fraud charges leading to imprisonment.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Funding the Canadian entity with excessive shareholder debt from a specified non-resident (debt-to-equity exceeding 1.5:1) or back-to-back loans, converting taxable income into deductible interest and thereby avoiding dividend WHT.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Interest deduction denied under ITA s.18(4); EIFEL may further disallow net interest above the 30% EBITDA threshold; GAAR may apply to back-to-back arrangements; 25% WHT imposed on disguised distributions.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who structured the financing with a tax-indifferent lender are jointly liable for the resulting corporate tax deficiency under Queensland/equitable trust principles where funds were diverted; criminal neglect findings trigger fines and travel bans.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: AML / FINTRAC Non-Compliance on Payment Rails
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Using Wise B2B or wire-transfer payment rails to collect or transmit funds on behalf of clients without registering as a Money Services Business (MSB) with FINTRAC, if such activity constitutes money transferring as a business; implementing unreported retail foreign-exchange or remittance flows.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Administrative monetary penalties under the PCMLTFA up to CAD 1,000,000 for corporations and CAD 500,000 for individuals; criminal prosecution for wilfully failing to report suspicious transactions or to implement the AML compliance program.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who knowingly direct or authorize unregistered MSB activity are personally liable for fines and, under criminal AML provisions, imprisonment of up to 10 years; restitution orders and travel bans apply pending prosecution; CRA may also deny deductions for income from the unlicensed activity.
